subject: maths
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Single-event probability from equally likely outcomes
Probabilities of all outcomes summing to 1
Sample spaces for single and combined events
Sets, unions, intersections and Venn diagrams

questions.q: Which of these could NOT be a probability?
questions.explain: Every probability lies between 0 and 1 inclusive. 1.2 is greater than 1, so it is impossible for it to be a probability.

questions.q: An event has probability 0.85. Which word best describes it?
options: Impossible
Unlikely
Likely
Certain
questions.explain: 0.85 is close to 1 but not equal to it, so the event is likely but not certain. Certain would be exactly 1.

questions.lo: Single-event probability from equally likely outcomes
questions.q: A fair dice is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
questions.explain: Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, so 2 favourable outcomes out of 6. P = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.lo: Single-event probability from equally likely outcomes
questions.q: A bag has 5 red, 3 blue and 2 yellow counters. One is taken at random. What is P(red)?

questions.lo: Single-event probability from equally likely outcomes
questions.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, red, blue, green. Josh says 'there are 3 colours so P(blue) = 1/3.' What is P(blue) really?
questions.explain: There are 4 equal sections and only 1 is blue, so P(blue) = 1/4. The number of colours is not the number of equally likely outcomes.

questions.lo: Probabilities of all outcomes summing to 1
questions.q: The probability it rains tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability it does NOT rain?
questions.explain: Raining and not raining are the only outcomes and are mutually exclusive, so they sum to 1. P(not rain) = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7.

questions.lo: Probabilities of all outcomes summing to 1
questions.q: A spinner lands on A, B or C only. P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.2. What is P(C)?
questions.explain: All outcomes sum to 1, so P(C) = 1 - 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3.

questions.q: For one roll of a fair dice, which pair of events is MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE (they cannot both happen)?
options: Rolling an even number and rolling a 4
Rolling a 6 and rolling an even number
Rolling a 2 and rolling a 5
Rolling an odd number and rolling a 3
questions.explain: Rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 cannot both happen on one roll, so they are mutually exclusive. In the other pairs one event can happen at the same time as the other (e.g. a 4 is even).

questions.q: A fair dice is rolled. Rolling a 1 and rolling a 2 are mutually exclusive. What is P(rolling a 1 OR a 2)?
questions.explain: For mutually exclusive events you add the probabilities: 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.q: A drawing pin is dropped 50 times and lands point-up 30 times. What is the experimental probability (relative frequency) of point-up?
The experimental probability a machine makes a faulty part is 0.05. In a batch of 400 parts, how many would you expect to be faulty?
questions.explain: Expected number = probability x trials = 0.05 x 400 = 20.

questions.q: A student flips a fair coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. Which statement is correct?
options: The coin must be biased
The theoretical probability of heads is still 0.5
The experimental probability equals the theoretical probability
Heads is now more likely than tails on the next flip
questions.explain: Short experiments are noisy, so 7 heads in 10 does not prove bias. The theoretical probability of heads on a fair coin stays 0.5 each flip.

questions.q: As you increase the number of trials in an experiment, the relative frequency usually...
options: moves further from the theoretical probability
gets closer to the theoretical probability
stays exactly the same
always equals exactly the theoretical probability
questions.explain: With more trials, experimental results tend to settle towards the true (theoretical) probability.

questions.lo: Sample spaces for single and combined events
questions.q: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.explain: Each dice has 6 outcomes, so together there are 6 x 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes.

questions.lo: Sample spaces for single and combined events
questions.q: Two fair dice are rolled. Using the sample space of 36 outcomes, what is the probability the total is 7?

questions.lo: Sets, unions, intersections and Venn diagrams
questions.q: In a Venn diagram, what does the overlap (intersection) of two sets show?
options: Members in neither set
Members in the first set only
Members in both sets
Members in either set
questions.explain: The intersection is the region belonging to both sets at once. 'Either set' would be the union (everything in at least one).

questions.lo: Sets, unions, intersections and Venn diagrams
questions.q: In a class of 30, 12 study only French, 7 study both French and Spanish, 6 study only Spanish and 5 study neither. How many study at least one language?
questions.explain: 'At least one' is the union: 12 + 7 + 6 = 25 students.

questions.lo: Sets, unions, intersections and Venn diagrams
questions.q: Using the same class of 30 (12 only French, 7 both, 6 only Spanish, 5 neither), a student is chosen at random. What is the probability they study Spanish (including both)?
questions.explain: Studying Spanish means the whole Spanish circle: 7 (both) + 6 (only Spanish) = 13. P = 13/30.
